events.fact: Former Vice President Aaron Burr was acquitted of treason at Richmond, where Chief Justice John Marshall held that the Constitution's strict standard of an overt act had not been met.
American oceanographer Robert Ballard and his Woods Hole team located the wreck of the Titanic two and a half miles down in the North Atlantic after years of searching.

block: On September 1, 1807, former Vice President Aaron Burr was acquitted of treason at Richmond, where Chief Justice John Marshall refused to bend the Constitution's strict demand for an overt act even against a man widely despised. On the same day in 1985, after years of patient searching, the American oceanographer Robert Ballard and his Woods Hole team at last found the wreck of the Titanic resting two and a half miles beneath the North Atlantic. A Steadfast citizen holds his ground as Marshall held to the written law and as Ballard held to his quiet labor, trusting that what is faithfully pursued under God will in His time be brought to light.

events.fact: Union General William T. Sherman captured Atlanta after a long campaign, telegraphing Washington, 'Atlanta is ours, and fairly won.'
Japan signed the formal instrument of surrender aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay before General Douglas MacArthur, ending the Second World War.

block: On September 2, 1864, after months of grinding advance, Union General William T. Sherman took Atlanta and wired to Washington, 'Atlanta is ours, and fairly won.' On the same day in 1945, the long agony of the Second World War was ended when Japan signed the formal surrender on the deck of the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay before General Douglas MacArthur. Both victories were the fruit of years of weariness borne to the end, teaching a Steadfast citizen that the prize is given not to the swift but to the man who endures, looking to God for the strength to finish what he has begun.

events.fact: The Treaty of Paris was signed, by which Great Britain recognized the independence of the United States and ended the Revolutionary War.
NASA's Viking 2 lander touched down safely on the plains of Utopia Planitia, the second American spacecraft to land on Mars.

block: On September 3, 1783, the Treaty of Paris was signed in that city, and Great Britain at last acknowledged the independence the United States had bled eight years to secure. On the same day in 1976, NASA's Viking 2 settled gently onto the rust-colored plains of Mars, the second American craft to touch another world and send back its images across the void. From the long war won to the far planet reached, a Steadfast citizen learns that no worthy thing is gained quickly, and he labors on with patience, knowing the God who upholds the heavens rewards the man who does not grow weary.

events.fact: Spanish settlers founded the pueblo of Los Angeles in California with prayer and benediction, naming it El Pueblo de Nuestra Senora la Reina de los Angeles.
The Apache leader Geronimo surrendered to General Nelson Miles at Skeleton Canyon in Arizona, bringing the long Apache wars of the Southwest to a close.

block: On September 4, 1781, a band of forty-four settlers circled the chosen ground and, invoking God's blessing with prayer and benediction, founded the pueblo of Los Angeles in Spanish California. On the same day in 1886, Geronimo and his exhausted followers surrendered to General Nelson Miles in Skeleton Canyon, and the long, weary Apache wars of the Southwest came to their end at last. The patience that plants a town in the wilderness and the perseverance that sees a hard campaign through to peace alike call a Steadfast citizen to remain faithful in his post until the work is done, trusting the providence of God over every frontier.

events.fact: The First Continental Congress convened at Carpenters' Hall in Philadelphia, with delegates from twelve colonies gathering to seek a common redress of grievances.
The French fleet under Admiral de Grasse defeated the British at the Battle of the Chesapeake, sealing off the sea and making the victory at Yorktown possible.

block: On September 5, 1774, delegates from twelve colonies gathered at Carpenters' Hall in Philadelphia for the First Continental Congress, submitting their separate interests to common counsel for the good of all. On the same day in 1781, Admiral de Grasse and the French fleet bested the British at the Battle of the Chesapeake, and by holding the bay in disciplined order they shut the door of the sea on Cornwallis and made Yorktown's surrender certain. An Obedient citizen learns from both the hall and the harbor that strength is found in submitting himself to lawful order, and that the man who keeps his appointed place under authority serves a cause far greater than himself before God.

events.fact: The Marquis de Lafayette was born in Chavaniac, France; he would cross the sea as a young man to serve without pay under Washington in the cause of American liberty.
President William McKinley was shot by an anarchist at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo, New York, and would die of the wound eight days later.

block: On September 6, 1757, the Marquis de Lafayette was born in France, and as a young nobleman he would freely cross the ocean to serve without pay under General Washington, binding himself to a duty not his own by birth. On the same day in 1901, an anarchist's bullet struck President William McKinley at the Buffalo exposition, a wound from which he would die eight days afterward, meeting his end with quiet submission and forgiveness toward his killer. The willing service of Lafayette and the patient death of McKinley alike summon an Obedient citizen to take up the duty set before him and to bow, in life and in death, to the good and sovereign will of God.

events.fact: Spanish admiral Pedro Menendez de Aviles founded St. Augustine in Florida, the oldest continuously occupied European settlement in the present United States.
Dutch governor Peter Stuyvesant surrendered New Amsterdam to an English squadron without a shot fired, and the city was renamed New York.

block: On September 8, 1565, the Spanish admiral Pedro Menendez de Aviles planted St. Augustine on the Florida shore, the oldest enduring European settlement in what would become the United States. On the same day in 1664, Dutch governor Peter Stuyvesant yielded New Amsterdam to an English squadron without a single shot, and the city took the name New York under which it would grow into a great metropolis. The town that has stood unbroken for centuries and the city handed peaceably from one people to another both teach a Steadfast citizen to build on foundations meant to last, raising up what will outlive him for the glory of God and the good of those who follow.

events.fact: The Second Continental Congress resolved that the style of the new nation in all official acts should be the 'United States' in place of the 'United Colonies.'
California was admitted to the Union as the thirty-first state when President Millard Fillmore signed the act as part of the Compromise of 1850.

block: On September 9, 1776, the Continental Congress resolved that the people should henceforth be styled the 'United States' rather than the 'United Colonies,' fixing the name to which a nation would pledge its faith and honor. On the same day in 1850, California entered the Union as the thirty-first state by the hand of President Millard Fillmore, joining its fortunes to the compact of the whole. A Trustworthy citizen reverences both the name he bears and the bonds he enters, keeping covenant with his countrymen as one who knows that the God of truth holds men to the word they have given.

events.fact: Commodore Oliver Hazard Perry won the Battle of Lake Erie over a British squadron and reported, 'We have met the enemy and they are ours.'
Elias Howe received the first United States patent for a practical lockstitch sewing machine, the fruit of years of stubborn invention.

block: On September 10, 1813, Commodore Oliver Hazard Perry, his flagship shot to wreckage beneath him, shifted his banner to the Niagara, broke the British line on Lake Erie, and sent word, 'We have met the enemy and they are ours.' On the same day in 1846, after years bent over his workbench in poverty, Elias Howe was granted the first American patent for a practical lockstitch sewing machine that would clothe a nation. The captain who would not give up the ship and the inventor who would not give up his labor both show a Trustworthy citizen what it means to be relied upon, faithful in the post and at the bench until the charge is fulfilled before God and man.

events.fact: The Battle of Brandywine was fought in Pennsylvania, where Washington's outnumbered Continental Army was beaten by General Howe yet withdrew in order to fight again.

Terrorists hijacked four airliners and attacked the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, killing nearly three thousand; the passengers of Flight 93 gave their lives to bring their plane down in a Pennsylvania field.

block: On September 11, 1777, Washington's outnumbered army was defeated at Brandywine in Pennsylvania, yet his men withdrew in good order and rose to fight again rather than yield the cause. On the same day in 2001, hijacked airliners struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, taking nearly three thousand lives, while the men of Flight 93 obeyed a higher duty and forced their plane into a Pennsylvania field to spare others. In a dark hour, an Obedient citizen looks to the God who reigns over even our deepest griefs, and resolves like the soldier and the men aloft to do the next right thing whatever the cost.

events.fact: At the Battle of North Point near Baltimore, Maryland militia under General John Stricker delayed the British advance and bought precious time to fortify the city; Maryland keeps the day as Defenders' Day.
President John F. Kennedy declared at Rice University that the nation would go to the moon, 'not because they are easy, but because they are hard.'

block: On September 12, 1814, the Maryland militia under General John Stricker stood in the path of the British at North Point and, though pressed back, bought the hours Baltimore needed to brace its defenses, a stand the state still honors as Defenders' Day. On the same day in 1962, President John F. Kennedy told a crowd at Rice University that the nation would reach the moon, choosing that labor 'not because they are easy, but because they are hard.' A Steadfast citizen embraces hard things by deliberate choice, holding the line where he is set and bending his strength to great works, trusting that God honors the man who does not flinch from difficulty.

events.fact: The Confederation Congress passed the ordinance putting the new Constitution into operation, fixing the dates for the first federal elections and the start of the new government.
British warships opened a twenty-five-hour bombardment of Fort McHenry in Baltimore harbor, which the garrison endured without surrender.

block: On September 13, 1788, the Confederation Congress passed the ordinance that set the new Constitution into motion, appointing the dates for the first federal elections and the orderly birth of the government we still keep. On the same day in 1814, British warships began a twenty-five-hour bombardment of Fort McHenry, and through the long night of fire the garrison held the harbor and would not strike its flag. The ordered founding of a government and the unyielding defense of a fort alike teach a Steadfast citizen to stand firm under pressure, holding fast to what is good through the dark hours, confident that God watches over the faithful.

events.fact: Seeing the flag still flying over Fort McHenry at dawn, Francis Scott Key wrote the verses that became 'The Star-Spangled Banner.'
President William McKinley died of his assassin's wound, and Theodore Roosevelt was sworn in as president that same day in Buffalo, New York.

block: On September 14, 1814, when the smoke lifted and the great flag still flew above Fort McHenry, Francis Scott Key took up his pen and wrote the words that would become 'The Star-Spangled Banner.' On the same day in 1901, President William McKinley died of his wound, and Theodore Roosevelt at once took the oath of office at Buffalo, that the Republic might not be left without a steady hand. The flag that stood through the night and the orderly passing of the highest office in a single day both call a Steadfast citizen to keep his footing when others are shaken, trusting the unchanging God who carries a nation through its trials.

events.fact: The Mayflower set sail from Plymouth, England, bearing the Pilgrims across the Atlantic to plant a colony where they might worship God in freedom.
At the Battle of Harlem Heights in Manhattan, Washington's Continentals won their first battlefield success, restoring the army's confidence after the loss of New York.

block: On September 16, 1620, the Mayflower weighed anchor at Plymouth, England, carrying the Pilgrims out upon the open sea toward a wilderness where they purposed to worship God according to their consciences. On the same day in 1776, Washington's battered Continentals turned and won their first clear success at Harlem Heights, proving to themselves that they could face the British and stand. The faith that braved an ocean and the courage that held the field after defeat both summon a Steadfast citizen to press on through hardship, fixing his hope in the God who steadies the trembling hand and rewards the resolute heart.

events.fact: President George Washington laid the cornerstone of the United States Capitol in a ceremony on the new federal city's hill.
The United States Air Force was established as a separate military service under the National Security Act of 1947.

block: On September 18, 1793, President George Washington laid the cornerstone of the United States Capitol upon its hill, setting the first stone of the house where a free people's laws would be made. On the same day in 1947, the United States Air Force was raised up as a separate service, a new guardian of the skies for the defense of the Republic. The founding of a seat of government and the forming of a shield for the nation both teach a Steadfast citizen to build patiently for the long defense of liberty, laying sound foundations as before the God who endures from age to age.

events.fact: At the Battle of Freeman's Farm, the first clash at Saratoga, American forces under General Gates bloodied and halted General Burgoyne's invading British army in New York.
George Washington's Farewell Address was first published, counseling the nation toward union, faith, and morality as the pillars of its liberty.

block: On September 19, 1777, the first battle of Saratoga was fought at Freeman's Farm, where General Gates and his men checked General Burgoyne's advance through New York and turned the tide of the war. On the same day in 1796, George Washington's Farewell Address was first printed, in which the departing president urged his countrymen to cherish union and to hold religion and morality as the indispensable supports of their freedom. The line that held at Saratoga and the wise counsel of a faithful leader both call a Steadfast citizen to guard what his fathers secured, standing firm in battle and in virtue under the eye of Almighty God.

events.fact: The frigate USS Constitution, later famed as 'Old Ironsides,' was sent down the ways in her launching ceremony at Boston before President John Adams.
At the Battle of Chickamauga in Georgia, General George H. Thomas held his ground against the Confederate onslaught and earned the name 'the Rock of Chickamauga.'

block: On September 20, 1797, the frigate that would be called 'Old Ironsides' began her launching at Boston before President John Adams, the USS Constitution that endures afloat to this day. On the same day in 1863, when the Union line broke at Chickamauga in Georgia, General George H. Thomas planted himself on the ridge and held against every assault, winning forever the name 'the Rock of Chickamauga.' The ship that would not be sunk and the general who would not be moved alike show a Trustworthy citizen what it is to be depended upon in the worst hour, standing fast for others as a rock set firm by the hand of God.

events.fact: Frank Duryea road-tested in Springfield, Massachusetts the gasoline automobile built with his brother Charles, among the first successful American motorcars.
The Great New England Hurricane, the 'Long Island Express,' struck without warning, taking hundreds of lives and devastating the coast of the Northeast.

block: On September 21, 1893, Frank Duryea drove the gasoline carriage he and his brother Charles had built through the streets of Springfield, Massachusetts, and though it stalled at first he mended it and ran on, launching the American automobile. On the same day in 1938, the Great New England Hurricane roared in with little warning, claiming hundreds of lives and laying waste the northern coast before the survivors set themselves to rebuild. The inventor who pressed on after his machine failed and the stricken towns that rose again from the storm both teach a Steadfast citizen to endure the sudden blow and labor on, casting himself upon the God who is a refuge in the day of trouble.

events.fact: Captain Nathan Hale was hanged by the British in New York as a spy, going to his death with calm courage in the service of his country.
President Abraham Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, declaring that the enslaved in the rebelling states would be free on the first day of the new year.

block: On September 22, 1776, the young schoolmaster Captain Nathan Hale was hanged by the British as a spy in New York, meeting his death with a composure long remembered as the mark of a patriot who counted his life well spent for his country. On the same day in 1862, President Abraham Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, binding himself and the nation to set free the enslaved within the rebellious states. The soldier obedient unto death and the president heeding the demand of conscience alike call an Obedient citizen to submit himself to the higher law, doing the right that is set before him whatever it costs, in the fear of God.

events.fact: Off Flamborough Head, Captain John Paul Jones of the Bonhomme Richard, asked if he would surrender, by tradition replied, 'I have not yet begun to fight,' and went on to capture the British frigate Serapis.
The Lewis and Clark expedition returned to St. Louis after two and a half years, having crossed the continent to the Pacific and back.

block: On September 23, 1779, with his ship aflame and sinking beneath him off the English coast, Captain John Paul Jones answered the call to surrender, by tradition, 'I have not yet begun to fight,' and fought on until the British Serapis struck her colors to him. On the same day in 1806, Meriwether Lewis and William Clark brought their Corps of Discovery home to St. Louis after two and a half years, having pressed across the unmapped continent to the Pacific and returned. The captain who would not quit a burning deck and the explorers who would not turn back from the wilderness both teach a Steadfast citizen to hold to his purpose to the very end, trusting the God who strengthens those who do not faint.

events.fact: John Marshall, the great Chief Justice who would establish the authority of the Supreme Court, was born in a log cabin in Germantown, Virginia.
President George Washington signed the Judiciary Act of 1789, establishing the federal court system and the Supreme Court of the United States.

block: On September 24, 1755, John Marshall was born in a Virginia log cabin, the man who as Chief Justice would give the Supreme Court its enduring strength and root the rule of law deep in the new nation. On the very same day in 1789, President George Washington signed the Judiciary Act, raising up the federal courts and the Supreme Court that Marshall would one day lead. That the great judge and the court he would steady share one calendar day is a quiet providence, calling a Steadfast citizen to honor the patient framework of justice and to do his own part faithfully, knowing the God of order builds His purposes through ordinary men.

events.fact: The first newspaper in the American colonies, 'Publick Occurrences Both Forreign and Domestick,' was printed in Boston, though the authorities suppressed it after a single issue.
Congress approved twelve proposed amendments and sent them to the states; ten of them would be ratified as the Bill of Rights.

block: On September 25, 1690, the first newspaper in the American colonies, 'Publick Occurrences,' was printed in Boston, and though the authorities silenced it after one issue, the longing for a free press it kindled would not die. On the same day in 1789, Congress approved twelve amendments and sent them out to the states, ten of which would endure as the Bill of Rights that still guards American liberty. The suppressed sheet whose cause outlived it and the charter of freedoms written for the generations both call an Enduring citizen to labor for what will long outlast him, sowing in his own day what God will bring to harvest in years he may never see.

events.fact: John Chapman, remembered as Johnny Appleseed, was born in Leominster, Massachusetts; he would spend his life planting orchards across the frontier.
The Senate unanimously confirmed John Jay as the first Chief Justice of the United States, and President Washington sealed his commission that day.

block: On September 26, 1774, John Chapman, the man known as Johnny Appleseed, was born in Massachusetts, and he would walk the frontier for decades planting orchards whose fruit he would never gather for himself. On the same day in 1789, the Senate gave its unanimous voice to John Jay as the first Chief Justice of the United States, and Washington sealed his commission, setting a faithful man at the head of the new courts. The nurseryman scattering seed for those who came after and the founding of a steady bench of justice both teach a Steadfast citizen to do quiet, lasting good in his appointed place, content to serve the purposes of God beyond his own lifetime.

events.fact: Samuel Adams, the Boston patriot and signer of the Declaration of Independence, was born; he became a tireless organizer of colonial resistance.
The Continental Congress appointed John Adams as minister to negotiate peace and commerce with Great Britain, a charge that would help secure favorable terms at Paris.

block: On September 27, 1722, Samuel Adams was born in Boston, the steadfast patriot whose tireless labors knit the colonies together in resistance and who would set his name to the Declaration of Independence. On the same day in 1779, the Continental Congress named his cousin John Adams to negotiate peace and commerce with Britain, a duty he would carry across the sea and which helped win the favorable terms of the Treaty of Paris. The kinsmen Adams, one stirring a people to liberty and the other patiently securing its peace, alike call a Steadfast citizen to lifelong constancy in his duty, serving his country through long years as a faithful steward under God.

events.fact: Juan Rodriguez Cabrillo sailed into San Diego Bay, becoming the first European to explore the coast of present-day California.
General Washington's combined American and French army arrived before Yorktown and laid siege to Cornwallis, beginning the campaign that won American independence.

block: On September 28, 1542, Juan Rodriguez Cabrillo brought his small fleet into the harbor he named San Miguel, today's San Diego Bay, the first European to chart the coast of California. On the same day in 1781, General Washington and his allied American and French army arrived before Yorktown and laid the siege that would force Cornwallis to surrender and seal American independence. The explorer venturing into unknown waters and the army settling in for the patient work of a siege both teach a Steadfast citizen to set his face toward the hard task and see it through, trusting the God who crowns persevering labor with its end.
